## Sleep Duration Impact on Daily Physical Activity

### Question: Why Do We Sleep?

![](https://media4.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExNWc5dXgzMXA5aWE4am95cDlmbnY0Mm5jbHpmZm82bzc2M2RjcXl3bCZlcD12MV9pbnRlcm5hbF9naWZfYnlfaWQmY3Q9Zw/mkhMTALnrYRLnuoe5P/giphy.gif)


Sleep impacts various aspects of our life ranging from daily performances, physical and mental well being to cognitive functions. <br> <br>
In this report we will explore how sleep duration affects daily physical activity.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
# Read csv file data into data frame
logged_data <- read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vTYFL_2sQj4V1Oh7M2WdHTJk2IOEFcffXXOGsNaGJUfF3s7tHrDZpguYu6NCTO1LqTR5vvlP5OcQYvi/pub?gid=1367836881&single=true&output=csv") %>%
  # Use a pipe to pass the data frame into rename() to rename the variables of logged_data
  rename(sleep_category = 2, exercise_category = 3, step_category = 4, active_calories_burnt = 5) 


# Plots and numeric summaries are used in the final report -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Create an ordered factor for sleep categories to display visual order in the plot
ordered_logged_data <- logged_data %>%
  mutate(sleep_factor = factor(sleep_category, 
                                 levels = c("Very little (Less than 4 hours)",
                                            "Little (4 hours to 6 hours)",
                                            "Moderate (6 hours to 8 hours)",
                                            "Enough (8 to 10 hours)",
                                            "A lot (More than 10 hours)")))

```

### Plot 1 - Exercise Distribution Across Sleep Duration Categories

```{r fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}


# This plot displays exercise distribution across sleep duration categories
exercise_distribution_plot <- ordered_logged_data %>%
  ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = sleep_factor, fill = exercise_category)) +
  labs(title = "Exercise Distribution Across Sleep Duration Categories",
       subtitle = "Exploring how different amounts of sleep duration relate to daily exercise levels",
       caption = "Source: Stats 220 Survey responses (Apple Health & Fitness Apps)",
       y = "Sleep Category",
       x = "Number of Sleep Observations")

# Call the function to display plot
exercise_distribution_plot

```


This plot displays how exercise levels are distributed across different sleep duration categories. <br> <br>
Overall, individuals with **moderate to a lot** of sleep appear to have a **higher** frequency of **moderate to high** exercise levels, while those with **very little or little** sleep tend to show **lower** levels of exercise. 
<br> <br>
This suggests a potential relationship between **longer sleep duration and higher levels of exercise.**


### Plot 2 - Distribution of Step Counts Across Sleep Duration Categories


```{r fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}

# This plot displays step count distribution across sleep duration categories
step_count_distribution_plot <- ordered_logged_data %>%
  ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(aes(y = sleep_factor, fill = step_category)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Step Counts Across Sleep Duration Categories",
       subtitle = "Exploring how different amounts of sleep duration relate to daily step counts",
       caption = "Source: Stats 220 Survey responses (Apple Health & Fitness Apps)",
       y = "Sleep Category",
       x = "Number of Sleep Observations")

# Call the function to display plot
step_count_distribution_plot


```


This plot displays how step count categories are distributed across different sleep duration categories. 
<br> <br>
Individuals with **moderate to a lot** of sleep tend to have **higher** step count categories. 
<br> <br>
This suggests a potential relationship between **longer sleep duration and increased daily movement.**


```{r}

# Observation count of each sleep category
sleep_counts <- table(logged_data$sleep_category)

# Most common sleep category
most_common_sleep_category <- names(sleep_counts)[which.max(sleep_counts)]

# Sleep category with the highest frequency
max_sleep_count <- max(sleep_counts)


```

The most common sleep category was `r most_common_sleep_category`, with `r max_sleep_count` observations.
